cards.back: A departure from what is normal or expected; an anomaly. "The sudden drop in temperature was an aberration for this time of year." Common collocations: statistical aberration, mental aberration, temporary aberration.

To deliberately choose not to do or have something; to refrain. "Several members chose to abstain from voting on the controversial proposal." Common collocations: abstain from alcohol, abstain from voting, abstain from eating.

To make something more noticeable or prominent; to emphasize. "The report accentuates the need for immediate reform in the education sector." Common collocations: accentuate the positive, accentuate differences, accentuate the problem.

An award or privilege granted as a special honour or acknowledgement of merit. "Receiving the Nobel Prize is considered the highest accolade in the scientific community." Common collocations: receive an accolade, highest accolade, prestigious accolade.

To stick firmly to a surface, or to follow rules or beliefs closely. "All participants must adhere to the guidelines outlined in the handbook." Common collocations: adhere to rules, adhere to principles, strictly adhere.

A difficult or unpleasant situation; hardship or misfortune. "Communities often demonstrate remarkable resilience in the face of adversity." Common collocations: face adversity, overcome adversity, in times of adversity.

Concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty; relating to visual appearance. "The architect prioritised the aesthetic appeal of the building without compromising functionality." Common collocations: aesthetic value, aesthetic appeal, aesthetic pleasure.

A natural liking for or attraction to a person, thing, or idea; a similarity in structure. "She has always had a strong affinity for languages and picked up Mandarin quickly." Common collocations: natural affinity, strong affinity, affinity for something.

To make suffering, a problem, or a deficiency less severe. "The new policy aims to alleviate poverty in the most disadvantaged regions." Common collocations: alleviate pain, alleviate suffering, alleviate pressure.

To combine or unite to form one organisation or structure; to merge. "The two companies decided to amalgamate in order to compete more effectively in the global market." Common collocations: amalgamate resources, amalgamate ideas, amalgamate into one.

Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something or someone. "Many voters remain ambivalent about the proposed changes to the healthcare system." Common collocations: feel ambivalent, ambivalent attitude, ambivalent about something.

To make something bad or unsatisfactory better; to improve. "Significant investment is required to ameliorate the living conditions in overcrowded urban areas." Common collocations: ameliorate conditions, ameliorate the situation, ameliorate suffering.

Comparable in certain respects; similar or equivalent in function or position. "The relationship between a teacher and student is analogous to that of a mentor and apprentice." Common collocations: analogous to, analogous situation, broadly analogous.

Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected; an irregularity. "Researchers identified an anomaly in the data that could not be explained by the existing model." Common collocations: statistical anomaly, detect an anomaly, apparent anomaly.

Anxiety or fear that something bad or unpleasant will happen. "There is growing apprehension among residents about the potential impact of the new factory." Common collocations: sense of apprehension, growing apprehension, with some apprehension.

To express an idea or feeling fluently and coherently; also, having clear and effective speech. "The candidate was able to articulate her vision for the future with remarkable clarity." Common collocations: articulate a vision, articulate clearly, articulate thoughts.

To find out something for certain; to determine or verify through investigation. "The committee was formed to ascertain the cause of the structural failure." Common collocations: ascertain the facts, ascertain the truth, difficult to ascertain.

To absorb and integrate information, ideas, or culture; to become part of a group. "It can take years for immigrants to fully assimilate into a new cultural environment." Common collocations: assimilate information, assimilate into society, assimilate knowledge.

To make something greater by adding to it; to increase or supplement. "The university plans to augment its online course offerings to reach a wider audience." Common collocations: augment income, augment reality, augment resources.

To prevent or ward off an undesirable occurrence; to turn away. "Swift diplomatic intervention helped to avert a full-scale military conflict." Common collocations: avert a crisis, avert disaster, avert one's eyes.

Well-meaning and kindly; showing goodwill and a desire to help others. "The benevolent organisation has provided clean water to over fifty villages in the region." Common collocations: benevolent society, benevolent dictator, benevolent act.

Concise and exact use of words in writing or speech; shortness of time or duration. "The professor was known for the brevity of his lectures, never exceeding thirty minutes." Common collocations: brevity of life, for the sake of brevity, with brevity.

Truthful and straightforward; frank and open in expression. "The minister gave a remarkably candid interview about the failures of the previous administration." Common collocations: candid opinion, candid assessment, candid conversation.

To cease to resist an opponent or an unwelcome demand; to surrender or give in. "After months of negotiation, the company finally capitulated to the workers' demands." Common collocations: forced to capitulate, capitulate to pressure, refuse to capitulate.

A person or thing that precipitates an event or change; something that speeds up a process. "The economic downturn acted as a catalyst for widespread political reform." Common collocations: act as a catalyst, catalyst for change, powerful catalyst.

To find a way around an obstacle or restriction; to overcome a problem cleverly. "Some corporations attempt to circumvent tax regulations by establishing subsidiaries abroad." Common collocations: circumvent the law, circumvent restrictions, circumvent the problem.

To persuade someone to do something by using force or threats; to compel. "No individual should be coerced into signing a contract they do not fully understand." Common collocations: coerce someone into, coerce compliance, coerced confession.

Clear, logical, and convincing; presenting a strong and persuasive argument. "The lawyer presented a cogent argument that ultimately swayed the jury's decision." Common collocations: cogent argument, cogent reasoning, cogent explanation.

Logical and consistent; forming a unified and understandable whole. "The essay lacked a coherent structure, making it difficult for readers to follow the argument." Common collocations: coherent strategy, coherent argument, coherent plan.

Corresponding in size, degree, or extent; proportionate. "Employees expect salaries that are commensurate with their level of experience." Common collocations: commensurate with experience, commensurate with effort, commensurate salary.

Evoking interest or attention in a powerfully irresistible way; convincing. "The documentary presents compelling evidence that climate change is accelerating." Common collocations: compelling argument, compelling evidence, compelling reason.

Naturally accompanying or associated with something; occurring together. "Rapid urbanisation and the concomitant rise in pollution have become major concerns." Common collocations: concomitant increase, concomitant risk, concomitant with.

To accept or allow behaviour that is considered wrong or offensive to continue. "The university does not condone any form of academic dishonesty, including plagiarism." Common collocations: condone violence, cannot condone, condone behaviour.

Making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible; favourable to. "A quiet and well-organised workspace is conducive to higher levels of productivity." Common collocations: conducive to learning, conducive environment, conducive to growth.

An opinion or conclusion formed on the basis of incomplete information; a guess. "Without further evidence, any explanation at this stage remains mere conjecture." Common collocations: pure conjecture, matter of conjecture, based on conjecture.

To make something stronger or more solid; to combine into a single more effective whole. "The government sought to consolidate its power by merging several ministries." Common collocations: consolidate power, consolidate gains, consolidate resources.

Standing out so as to be clearly visible; attracting notice or attention. "The conspicuous absence of the CEO from the annual meeting raised concerns." Common collocations: conspicuous absence, conspicuous consumption, conspicuous by its absence.

To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding with additional evidence. "The witness testimony helped to corroborate the evidence presented by the prosecution." Common collocations: corroborate evidence, corroborate a story, corroborate findings.

To reach a climax or point of highest development; to end with a particular result. "Years of dedicated research culminated in the discovery of a groundbreaking new treatment." Common collocations: culminate in, culminate with, efforts culminated.

To reduce in extent or quantity; to cut short or impose a restriction on. "The government introduced measures to curtail public spending during the financial crisis." Common collocations: curtail spending, curtail freedom, curtail activities.
A scarcity or lack of something. "There is a dearth of affordable housing in many major cities around the world." Common collocations: dearth of information, dearth of evidence, dearth of talent.

Tending to weaken or impair the strength or energy of something; causing serious harm. "Chronic stress can have a debilitating effect on both mental and physical health." Common collocations: debilitating illness, debilitating effect, debilitating condition.

To succeed in understanding or interpreting something that is unclear or difficult to read. "Historians spent decades trying to decipher the ancient script found on the stone tablets." Common collocations: decipher a code, decipher the meaning, difficult to decipher.

Polite submission and respect shown towards another person, often due to their position. "Out of deference to the elder members, the chairman postponed the vote." Common collocations: in deference to, show deference, out of deference.

To describe or portray something precisely; to indicate the exact position of a boundary. "The report clearly delineates the responsibilities of each department." Common collocations: delineate boundaries, clearly delineate, delineate the difference.

To publicly declare to be wrong or evil; to condemn openly. "Human rights organisations were quick to denounce the decision to restrict press freedom." Common collocations: denounce violence, publicly denounce, denounce as illegal.

To use up the supply or resources of something; to diminish in quantity. "Overfishing continues to deplete marine populations at an alarming rate." Common collocations: deplete resources, deplete reserves, severely depleted.

Tending to cause harm; damaging or injurious. "Excessive screen time has been shown to have a detrimental impact on children's development." Common collocations: detrimental effect, detrimental to health, detrimental impact.

A division or contrast between two things that are represented as being opposed or entirely different. "The dichotomy between urban wealth and rural poverty remains a pressing issue." Common collocations: false dichotomy, sharp dichotomy, dichotomy between.

To perceive or recognise something that is not immediately obvious; to distinguish. "It is increasingly difficult to discern reliable information from misinformation online." Common collocations: discern a pattern, difficult to discern, discern the difference.
